title: The traveler's hymns
hookLine: a Guru on the road east, and a hymn that asks the mind to take shelter

cards: Dust on the road. A river to cross by boat, then another. Days of walking and riding, nights in the homes of strangers who become sangat by morning.
Sikh tradition remembers Guru Tegh Bahadur as a traveler, journeying east toward Bengal and Assam, visiting Sikhs and meeting seekers along the way.
Tradition says his son, the future tenth Guru, was born at Patna while he was away on those journeys. A Guru on the road, far from home. And some of his hymns, tradition says, belong to those roads.

teach.h: ARRANGED BY RAGA, NOT BY PLACE.
teach.b: First, an honest thing. The Guru Granth Sahib arranges his hymns by raga, by musical mode, not by place.
There's no map beside each one, so when people link a hymn to a journey, that's tradition and memory, not a label in the book. But listen to what his hymns sound like, and the road is there.
One, in Raga Sorath, paraphrased, begins: O mind, take the shelter of the Lord's Name; remembering it, bad thinking is destroyed, and the highest state is reached. Shelter: in Gurmukhi, ot.
On a long road you don't need a palace; you need somewhere to stand out of the rain. And notice who the hymn talks to. Not the crowd, not a king.
O mind. It turns to the one companion who comes on every journey, the voice in your own head, often the only one listening.
So a traveler's hymn is a hymn you can carry: no building required, no instrument, no gathering. Just a line, and a mind to say it to.

This week has traveled too: Guru Arjan the editor and his whole life, then the ninth Guru's fearlessness, a home held lightly, their faith, their right, and a level heart. Different roads, one shelter.

how: Gurdwaras stand at places tradition links to Guru Tegh Bahadur's journeys, including Patna Sahib, and Sikhs sing his hymns in kirtan; some Sikhs also recite or listen to gurbani while traveling.

games.q: you're far from home for weeks, no gurdwara nearby, no instrument, no sangat. how do you keep praying?
o: carry a line, and speak it to your own mind.
find the nearest grand building first.
games.why: the ninth Guru's hymns speak to the mind: O mind, take shelter in the Name. a hymn you can carry anywhere.

practice: Ride your next trip in your mind, even a short one, the drive to work, the bus, the walk to the store, and pick one spot on the route to be your shelter: a light, a corner, a bridge.
Picture reaching it and speaking to your own mind for one breath. If you pray, the word can be Waheguru; if you don't, simply: here, now.
